Issued at 407 PM EDT Wed Jul 22 2026

PATTERN SYNOPSIS/FORECAST:

Northwest flow remains intact across the Midwest...with negatively 
tilted ridge axis from the PacNW into TX...and longwave trough axis 
stretching from Hudson Bay to New England. 100+kt jet stretches from 
southern Manitoba to the Mid-Atlantic...and then up along into Maine 
on the downstream side of the trough axis. Atmosphere is quite 
perturbed along/north of the jet axis, from the Canadian Prairie 
Provinces down into the Great Lakes; notably, a swirly dropping 
toward Lake Superior as of 12z and departing PV maxima over 
Ontario/Quebec. Dry air settling into the Lower Great Lakes/OH 
Valley attm with dewpoints falling into the mid to upper 40s 
overnight last night; best absolute moisture (pwats greater than 
1.5in) across the Gulf Coast up into New England along/ahead of the 
aforementioned trough axis and attendant cold front stretching from 
an occluded low over Quebec down along the Appalachian Mountains and 
into the southern Plains. Much cooler air mass beneath the trough as 
well...850mb temps as cold as 4C northeast of Georgian Bay, and 8C 
isotherm stretching from MN to the Lower Great Lakes. Lows generally 
bottoming out in the lower to middle 50s for a change last night, 
though. Northwest flow pressure gradient remains somewhat tight 
across the area, between aforementioned 993mb occluded low over 
Quebec and 1021mb surface high over the Upper Midwest/Northern 
Plains. A little smoke well aloft drifting overhead, as evidenced by 
visible satellite this morning, though not nearly as thick or 
impactful as previous days. 

High pressure will continue to build in into tonight; expect a cool 
and quiet night as winds diminish. Upper level pattern flattens out 
upstream Thursday, with a bit more influence of return flow to come 
into play here, and temps warming back up to more seasonable levels. 
May need to watch out for some warm advection activity Thursday 
night into Friday as a surface low tries to take shape across 
central Canada. Another lobe of energy sweeps through on 
Saturday...with ridging building over the western US ahead of 
troughing digging off British Columbia. Expecting height rises to 
spread eastward overall Sunday into Monday, with broad ridge axis 
centered to our west...but do have concerns for activity to form 
along the perimeter of the ridge at times. Increasing uncertainty in 
the forecast for Tuesday and beyond...depending on the 
strength/position of PV maxima tracking over the ridge axis...as 
well as position/strength of upper troughing progged to hang out 
over eastern Canada/northeastern US going into midweek, which will 
play a role in temperatures for next week. 

FORECAST DETAILS...

Lows tonight... Dewpoints this afternoon are already drying out 
quite a bit, generally into the lower 40s by 17z (with a couple 
spots diving down to 39F or lower (looking at you, APN, 
PZQ))...which is perhaps a bit more aggressive than guidance had 
suggested, and lends a concern for lows tonight. (Think this will 
also lend to a drier/less humid day on Thursday as well, and have 
gone much more aggressive with drying out dewpoints then, too.) Have 
thusly gone more aggressive with cooling temps tonight, given a good 
radiational cooling setup overall, with lows generally in the lower 
40s across the interior and warmer at the coasts; the typical 
interior cold spots (e.g., AuSable River valley) should drop close 
to 40, and would not be surprised to see a few sites come in with 
upper 30s tonight in those locales. The trick right now is how much 
lingering low-level moisture from recent rains will impact the lows 
tonight...and think the best chance of staying warmer (perhaps with 
some patchy fog?) will be NW Lower and the Leelanau Peninsula where 
they did have a couple inches of rain the other night (think this is 
part of what is driving slightly better diurnal cu coverage today 
over the western half of the Mitten). Not impossible some record low 
temperatures could be in jeopardy tonight...with most record lows 
this time of the year in the lower 40s (except for our coldest 
locales). Records at our primary historical weather sites are as 
follows: 

Record Low vs. current forecast....
Gaylord:          42 (1981) vs 41
Sault Ste. Marie: 39 (1981) vs 45
Houghton Lake:    35 (1947) vs 46
Traverse City:    42 (1985) vs 51
Alpena:           41 (1923) vs 45
Pellston:         35 (1985) vs 46
